passages.text: Non-Scanning Fiber-Optic Near-Infrared Beam Led to Two-Photon Optogenetic Stimulation <italic toggle="yes">In-Vivo</italic>

Stimulation of specific neurons expressing opsins in a targeted region to manipulate brain function has proved to be a powerful tool in neuroscience. <sentence_start/>However, the use of visible light for optogenetic stimulation is invasive due to low penetration depth and tissue damage owing to larger absorption and scattering. <sentence_start/>Here, we report, for the first time, in-depth non-scanning fiber-optic two-photon optogenetic stimulation (FO-TPOS) of neurons <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> in transgenic mouse models. <sentence_start/>In order to optimize the deep-brain stimulation strategy, we characterized two-photon activation efficacy at different near-infrared laser parameters. <sentence_start/>The significantly-enhanced in-depth stimulation efficiency of FO-TPOS as compared to conventional single-photon beam was demonstrated both by experiments and Monte Carlo simulation. <sentence_start/>The non-scanning FO-TPOS technology will lead to better understanding of the <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> neural circuitry because this technology permits more precise and less invasive anatomical delivery of stimulation.
Introduction

While neuronal imaging has enabled the mapping of the physical connectome <citation rid="pone.0111488-Seung1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2009.03.020" pmid="19376064" count="1">[1]</citation> of the brain in a high-throughput manner, there is now a growing need for an efficient, high resolution method to functionally map the multitude of neural connections in the brain. <sentence_start/>However, until recently, such a task was challenging not only in terms of the non-invasiveness, but also in the required cellular specificity in the sea of multifunctional neural units. <sentence_start/>Recently, visible light-assisted activation of selected neuronal group has been made possible with high temporal precision by introducing a light-activated molecular channel; channelrhodopsin-2 (ChR2) <citation rid="pone.0111488-Nagel1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="14615590" doi="10.1073/pnas.1936192100" pmcid="PMC283525" count="1">[2]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Boyden1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16116447" doi="10.1038/nn1525" count="1">[3]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Nagel2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16360690" doi="10.1016/j.cub.2005.11.032" count="1">[4]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Miller1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17170269" doi="10.1126/science.314.5806.1674" count="1">[5]</citation> and its variants. <sentence_start/>This method has several advantages over electrical stimulation <citation rid="pone.0111488-Christopher1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16510937" doi="10.1088/1741-2560/3/1/001" pmcid="PMC2583360" count="1">[6]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Butson1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16125463" doi="10.1016/j.clinph.2005.06.023" pmcid="PMC3653320" count="1">[7]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Voon1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16810676" doi="10.1002/mds.20963" count="1">[8]</citation> such as cellular specificity and minimal invasiveness and therefore, growing as a valuable tool in neuroscience research. <sentence_start/>Though the use of light-activated molecular ChR2 for <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> models is increasing, limitations of its utility exist. <sentence_start/>Although optogenetic methods require very low intensity light (a few mW/mm<sup>2</sup>) <citation rid="pone.0111488-Boyden1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="16116447" doi="10.1038/nn1525" count="1">[3]</citation>, at the activation wavelength for ChR2 (460 nm) significant absorption and scattering of stimulating light occurs which leads to limited (shallow) penetration of the beam <citation rid="pone.0111488-Cheong1" ref-type="bibr" count="1">[9]</citation> (Fig. 1a). <sentence_start/>Thus, in order to stimulate cells in the most ventral regions of the brain, one has to choose between one of two undesirable alternatives: The first is to maintain the minimally invasive qualities of the approach but requires that the average beam power be significantly increased. <sentence_start/>Unfortunately, this approach using single photon (visible) light often leads to significant deleterious effects on the cell viability in the vicinity of the target, and thus may limit the translational potential of this technology. <sentence_start/>The second alternative approach is to use optical fiber <citation rid="pone.0111488-Arenkiel1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17442243" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2007.03.005" pmcid="PMC3634585" count="1">[10]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Alexander1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="17873414" doi="10.1088/1741-2560/4/3/S02" count="1">[11]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Han1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19409264" doi="10.1016/j.neuron.2009.03.011" pmcid="PMC2830644" count="1">[12]</citation> or µLED <citation rid="pone.0111488-Cao1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/TBME.2012.2217395" pmid="22968201" count="1">[13]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Kim1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23580530" doi="10.1126/science.1232437" pmcid="PMC3769938" count="1">[14]</citation>-based blue light delivery to excite neurons in close proximity to the optical fiber or µLED. <sentence_start/>This approach may also compromise the minimally invasive qualities of optogenetics because optical fibers (similar to electrodes used in electrical stimulation techniques) or µLED(s) need to penetrate through more superficial brain tissue in order to reach more ventral brain regions. <sentence_start/>In this way, the more superficial brain tissue gets damaged; and such damage can lead to difficulty in interpreting the outcome of deep-brain stimulation. <sentence_start/>Therefore, several attempts have been made to shift the activation peak of ChR2 from the blue to the red wavelength region <citation rid="pone.0111488-Zhang1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18432196" doi="10.1038/nn.2120" pmcid="PMC2692303" count="1">[15]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Gunaydin1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20081849" doi="10.1038/nn.2495" count="1">[16]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Lin1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19254539" doi="10.1016/j.bpj.2008.11.034" pmcid="PMC2717302" count="1">[17]</citation>. <sentence_start/>While there has been some success at the cost of altered light-activation kinetics, it seems a near-infrared opsin would be ideal for in-depth cell-specific optogenetic stimulation of excitable cells in an organism. <sentence_start/>However, the success in developing a near-infrared opsin would still not permit applicability of the method for selective activation of small regions in deep (ventral) brain areas, since the single-photon (red or infrared) stimulating beam will also stimulate neurons outside of the targeted population (in the path of the beam, Fig. 1b).

Two-photon Optogenetic stimulation.

Schematic comparison: (a) single-photon blue excitation, (b) single-photon red-shifted excitation and (c) two-photon optogenetic stimulation (TPOS). <sentence_start/>(d) Intensity profile emanating from the multimode fiber, scale bar: 100 µm, (e) Spectrum of ultrafast tunable near-infrared fiber-optic beam, (f) Two-photon fluorescence (green) from polystyrene particle excited by multimode profile. <sentence_start/>In-vitro two-photon activation of ChR2-expressing cells with ultrafast NIR laser beam: (g) Representative current responses to ultrafast NIR laser beam at different wavelengths (in nm), (h) Fiber-optic two-photon activation spectrum at 0.02 mW/µm<sup>2</sup> (100 ms pulses).

Because of low absorption and scattering coefficients, the two-photon optogenetic activation using a near infrared laser beam can provide both deep penetration and high spatial precision, achieved by virtue of the non-linear nature of ultrafast light interaction with ChR2. <sentence_start/>Comparison of single-photon blue (a), and red-shifted excitation (b) with two-photon optogenetic stimulation (c) is shown in Fig. <sentence_start/>1. <sentence_start/>Since the first demonstration <citation rid="pone.0111488-Mohanty1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18621808" doi="10.1529/biophysj.108.130187" pmcid="PMC2553121" count="1">[18]</citation> of <italic toggle="yes">in-vitro</italic> two-photon optogenetic stimulation (TPOS) of ChR2-sensitized cells and neurons by using point or scanning laser beam, there has been significant progress <citation rid="pone.0111488-Rickgauer1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19706471" doi="10.1073/pnas.0907084106" pmcid="PMC2736443" count="1">[19]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Andrasfalvy1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20543137" doi="10.1073/pnas.1006620107" pmcid="PMC2900666" count="1">[20]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Papagiakoumou1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20852649" doi="10.1038/nmeth.1505" pmcid="PMC7645960" count="1">[21]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Packer1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23142873" doi="10.1038/nmeth.2249" pmcid="PMC3518588" count="1">[22]</citation> in using TPOS for probing neural circuitry in cultured neuronal cells as well as brain slices. <sentence_start/>Further, recent advances demonstrate that optogenetically-sensitized neurons can be activated by spatially-sculpting <citation rid="pone.0111488-Andrasfalvy1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20543137" doi="10.1073/pnas.1006620107" pmcid="PMC2900666" count="1">[20]</citation> and/or temporal-focusing <citation rid="pone.0111488-Papagiakoumou1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20852649" doi="10.1038/nmeth.1505" pmcid="PMC7645960" count="1">[21]</citation> the TPOS beam. <sentence_start/>It is important to note that the two-photon excitation has significant benefits over the single-photon excitation such as less photo-damage, enhanced penetration depth and localized stimulation <citation rid="pone.0111488-So1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="11701518" doi="10.1146/annurev.bioeng.2.1.399" count="1">[23]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Further, two-photon cross-section of ChR2 is empirically estimated <citation rid="pone.0111488-Rickgauer1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19706471" doi="10.1073/pnas.0907084106" pmcid="PMC2736443" count="1">[19]</citation> <sup>,</sup> <citation rid="pone.0111488-Papagiakoumou1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20852649" doi="10.1038/nmeth.1505" pmcid="PMC7645960" count="1">[21]</citation> to be larger than that of most of the fluorophores and therefore, has potential for stimulating opsin-expressing neurons using weakly-focused (and even defocused) two-photon beams. <sentence_start/>However, to date, two-photon excitation has only been demonstrated <italic toggle="yes">in-vitro</italic> with microscope-based setups <citation rid="pone.0111488-Mohanty1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18621808" doi="10.1529/biophysj.108.130187" pmcid="PMC2553121" count="1">[18]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Rickgauer1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19706471" doi="10.1073/pnas.0907084106" pmcid="PMC2736443" count="1">[19]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Shivalingaiah1" ref-type="bibr" count="1">[24]</citation> and recently by fiber-optic stimulation <citation rid="pone.0111488-Dhakal1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="23722792" doi="10.1364/OL.38.001927" count="1">[25]</citation>. <sentence_start/>Here, we demonstrate <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> fiber-optic two-photon optogenetic stimulation (FO-TPOS) of in-depth neuronal circuitry in transgenic mouse model. <sentence_start/>Our experiments, reported here, demonstrate that multimode fiber can be used: (1) <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> as a non-scanning beam unlike that used in earlier microscope objective based two-photon stimulation reports, (2) to achieve in-depth two-photon activation <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> and (3) to evaluate intensity and wavelength-dependent <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> fiber-optic two-photon optogenetic stimulation efficacy. <sentence_start/>Here, we would like to emphasize that this manuscript does not examine the axial localization ability of two-photon stimulation <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic>. <sentence_start/>Stimulation of ensemble of chemically-identical cells at large depths by two-photon fiber-optic optogenetic means as demonstrated here, in a non-invasive manner will enable dissecting the role of those ensembles in particular function and thus modulate behavior.
Materials and Methods
Ethics statement

All experimental procedures were conducted according to the University of Texas at Arlington-Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee approved protocol A10.009. <sentence_start/>The IACUC specifically approved this study.
Cell culture

HEK 293 cells were transfected with the ChR2-EYFP construct, cloned into pcDNA3.1 neo (Invitrogen, USA). <sentence_start/>ChR2 cDNA was kindly provided by Dr. Georg Nagel (University of Wuerzburg, Germany). <sentence_start/>EYFP was fused in-frame to the C-terminus of ChR2 by PCR. <sentence_start/>Transgene-expressing cells were identified by visualizing the EYFP fluorescence under suitable illumination (514 nm). <sentence_start/>Stable clones were selected with 200 mg/l G418 and colonies were picked after 2 weeks, and then expanded. <sentence_start/>Clones that showed the highest level of EYFP fluorescence were chosen for the optical activation experiments. <sentence_start/>Cells were maintained at 37°C, 5% CO<sub>2</sub> in DMEM containing 10% fetal bovine serum. <sentence_start/>For generating light activation, cells were loaded with all-trans retinal (1 µM) for at least 6 hours and activated with fiber-optic laser beam.
Optogenetic stimulation

For both the <italic toggle="yes">in-vitro</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> activation of ChR2-expressing cells (identified by YFP fluorescence) or different brain regions expressing ChR2, both two-photon and single photon sources coupled to a 50 µm core optical fiber using a fiber coupler (Newport Inc.), mounted on a mechanical micromanipulator so as to position the tip of the fiber near the region of interest. <sentence_start/>The single-photon source consists of a blue (473 nm, 30 mW) diode laser coupled to the fiber, while the two-photon beam is provided by a 200 fs near-infrared Ti: Sapphire laser (Maitai HP, Newport-SpectraPhysics Inc.) beam operating at ∼76 MHz, coupled to the same fiber. <sentence_start/>Further, the two-photon laser wavelength was tuned from 750 to 950 nm in order to compare the relative efficiencies of the various NIR wavelengths. <sentence_start/>Macro-exposure pulses of stimulation light were generated by a function generator driving the electro-mechanical shutter in the beam path. <sentence_start/>The function generator was synchronized to the <italic toggle="yes">in-vitro</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> electrophysiology recording system (Plexon and Biopac Inc.). <sentence_start/>Light power at the fiber-tip was measured using a standard light power meter (PM 100D, Thorlabs Inc).
Patch-clamp recording setup

The opto-electrophysiology set up was developed on an Olympus upright microscope platform using an amplifier system (Axon Multiclamp 700B, Molecular Devices Inc.). <sentence_start/>Parameters of the pipette puller were optimized in order to obtain desired borosilicate micropipettes of resistance from 3 to 5 MΩ for whole-cell patch clamp. <sentence_start/>The micropipette was filled with a solution containing (in mM) 130 K-Gluoconate, 7 KCl, 2 NaCl, 1 MgCl<sub>2</sub>, 0.4 EGTA, 10 HEPES, 2 ATP-Mg, 0.3 GTP-Tris and 20 sucrose. <sentence_start/>The electrode was mounted on a XYZ motorized micromanipulator (Newport Inc.). <sentence_start/>The standard extracellular solution containing (in mM): 150 NaCl, 10 Glucose, 5 KCl, 2 CaCl<sub>2</sub>, 1 MgCl<sub>2</sub> was buffered with 10 mM HEPES (pH 7.3). <sentence_start/>The output from the amplifier was digitized using a National Instruments card (PCI 6221). <sentence_start/>For electrophysiological recording, the hardware was interfaced with patch-clamp software from University of Strathclyde (non-commercial use). <sentence_start/>Electrical recordings were performed at a holding potential of −60 mV at room temperature (20-24°C). <sentence_start/>For activation of ChR2-expressing cells (identified by YFP fluorescence), the optogenetic stimulation beam (473 nm, or NIR) was delivered via a 50 µm core optical fiber, mounted on a mechanical micromanipulator so as to position the tip of the fiber near the desired cell being patch-clamped. <sentence_start/>For generating and controlling pulses of light, the electromechanical shutter in the laser beam path was interfaced with a PC. <sentence_start/>TTL pulses of desired frequency were generated using National Instruments (PCI 6221) card in order to generate required laser pulses for activation. <sentence_start/>For electrophysiological measurements subsequent to optical activation, the shutter was synchronized with the patch clamp recording electrode. <sentence_start/>The whole system was built on a vibration isolation table (Newport Inc.) and electrical isolation was done by means of a Faraday cage that was placed around the setup. <sentence_start/>pClamp software was used for data analysis.
Monte Carlo Simulation

Monte Carlo simulation is known as the most reliable and flexible method for modeling photon migration in biological tissue. <sentence_start/>Here, we used the widely-used Monte Carlo simulation codes for light propagation in multi-layered biological tissue named ‘MCML’ <citation rid="pone.0111488-Wang1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7587160" doi="10.1016/0169-2607(95)01640-f" count="1">[26]</citation> and ‘COV’ <citation rid="pone.0111488-Wang2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9421660" doi="10.1016/s0169-2607(97)00021-7" count="1">[27]</citation>. <sentence_start/>The brain was modeled as a two-layered tissue including grey matter and white matter. <sentence_start/>We set up parameters <citation rid="pone.0111488-Johansson1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="21054121" doi="10.1117/1.3495719" count="1">[28]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Yaroslavsky1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12118601" doi="10.1088/0031-9155/47/12/305" count="1">[29]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Cheong2" ref-type="bibr" count="1">[30]</citation> (µ<sub>a</sub> = absorption coefficient; µ<sub>s</sub> = scattering coefficient; g = anisotropy factor; n = refractive index, and d = thickness of cortical layers) as listed in Table S1 for the simulation, and then computed light propagation with the MCML code. <sentence_start/>Then the paired code ‘COV’ was utilized to extract the simulation output and calibrate the computed fluence rate distribution by quantitatively carrying the effect of Gaussian beam distribution and respective parameters, including beam size, laser power, and numerical aperture (NA). <sentence_start/>10<sup>7</sup> photons were launched in each simulation to achieve an excellent signal-to-noise ratio in simulation output <citation rid="pone.0111488-Wang1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="7587160" doi="10.1016/0169-2607(95)01640-f" count="1">[26]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Wang2" ref-type="bibr" pmid="9421660" doi="10.1016/s0169-2607(97)00021-7" count="1">[27]</citation>.
Mouse preparation

The (Thy1-ChR2-YFP) transgenic (n = 6, age between 12 to 16 weeks), and wild-type (C57BL/6J) mice (n = 3, age between 12 to 16 weeks) used in the reported experiments, were purchased from Jackson Labs. <sentence_start/>All aspects of experimental manipulation of our animals were in strict accordance with guidelines of the University of Texas at Arlington’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC). <sentence_start/>Mice were maintained on a 12∶12 light cycle (lights on at 07∶00).
<italic toggle="yes">In-vivo</italic> electrophysiology recordings

Animals were deeply anesthetized with 90 mg/kg ketamine and 10 mg/kg xylazine and placed in a stereotaxic frame (Kopf Instruments Inc.). <sentence_start/>For <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> recording, a linear midline skin incision was made and burr holes were bilaterally drilled in the skull at the anteroposterior (AP) (in reference to bregma) and mediolateral (ML) coordinates corresponding to VTA (−3.2 mm AP; ±0.5 mm ML). <sentence_start/>The electrode was implanted stereotaxically to allow recording from deep brain regions. <sentence_start/>Continuous electrical activity was then recorded either via a multichannel acquisition system (Omniplex, Plexon Inc.) or via an amplifier (MP-150, Biopac Inc.) interfaced with the Acqknowledge acquisition software on a networked PC. <sentence_start/>The animals were euthanized following electrophysiology recoding. <sentence_start/>by intraperitoneal injection of Sodium Pentobarbital (100 mg/kg).
Statistics

Data were analyzed using Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS, IBM). <sentence_start/>One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test was used to determine whether a significant difference occurred. <sentence_start/>The data were plotted as mean ± S. D. <sentence_start/>The accepted level of significance was <italic toggle="yes">p</italic><0.05.
Results
<italic toggle="yes">In-vitro</italic> fiber-optic near-infrared ultrafast laser irradiation leads to optogenetic stimulation

In contrast to the use of a microscope objective for focusing the two-photon laser beam, we employed a tunable (800-900 nm), ultrafast (200 fs) fiber-optic beam for non-scanning two-photon optogenetic activation. <sentence_start/>It is important to note here that earlier TPOS methods utilized different scanning modes (spiral, raster) for activation of ChR2-expressing cells to optimize the efficiency of excitation <citation rid="pone.0111488-Rickgauer1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19706471" doi="10.1073/pnas.0907084106" pmcid="PMC2736443" count="1">[19]</citation>. <sentence_start/>For testing the efficiency of fiber-based non-scanning two-photon activation <italic toggle="yes">in-vitro</italic>, HEK-293 cells expressing ChR2 were used and channel activities were recorded with patch clamp. <sentence_start/>The patch clamp set up for electrophysiological measurement subsequent to FO-TPOS is shown in Fig. <sentence_start/>S1a. <sentence_start/>The tunable Ti: Sapphire laser (FSL, 76 MHz) beam was expanded using a beam expander (BE) and coupled to an optical fiber using a lens (L). <sentence_start/>A shutter (S) controlled the exposure (macro-pulse) duration and a circular neutral density filter (NDF) was used to control the average beam power. <sentence_start/>In the case of single mode fiber-optic beam or laser beam focused by microscope objective, the intensity and, therefore, the two-photon stimulation is maximum at the center and slowly decays towards periphery (Gaussian nature). <sentence_start/>However, in case of the multimode fiber-optic beam, as used here, the maximum intensity spots are distributed over the irradiated cell(s) and two-photon stimulation is expected to occur in these spots leading to non-scanning activation of the cell(s). <sentence_start/>Fig. 1d shows the intensity profile of the NIR (875 nm) beam emanating from the multimode fiber at a distance of ∼1.3 mm from the cleaved end. <sentence_start/>In Fig. <sentence_start/>S1(e), we show the time-lapse (1 sec) intensity profiles (in different colors) along a line drawn across the beam profile (Fig. S1d). <sentence_start/>The beam profile was found to be stable (average correlation coefficient between two frames is 0.98) unless the fiber was mechanically actuated externally (Movie S1). <sentence_start/>In order to estimate the pulse width of the ultrafast NIR fiber-optic beam, the spectrum was measured using spectrometer (Ocean Optics Inc) at different wavelengths (Fig. 1e). <sentence_start/>At a fixed wavelength, variation of intensity (by changing the pump laser intensity) led to change in pulse width at lower pump power as shown in Fig. <sentence_start/>S1b. <sentence_start/>Since no significant change in pulse width at high oscillator power (1.3 to 1.7 W) was observed, this range was used for intensity-dependent studies. <sentence_start/>This range of oscillator IR laser power corresponds to ∼150 to 260 mW at the coupling end of the multimode fiber. <sentence_start/>With a coupling efficiency of nearly 50%, the average power at tip of the fiber was measured to be 75 to 130 mW. <sentence_start/>Before evaluating two-photon activation of cells by multimode fiber-optic beam, we examined if the ultrafast fiber-optic near-infrared beam has sufficient photon densities to result in two-photon excitation. <sentence_start/>Therefore, we carried out two-photon excitation of fluorescent polystyrene particles (Bangs Lab) by placing the cleaved fiber tip near the particles. <sentence_start/>The beam spot size is about 50 µm when the fiber was placed 10 µm away from the particles. <sentence_start/>Fig. 1f shows the green fluorescence emitted from 45 µm polystyrene particle(s) excited by the multimode fiber-optic beam (Movie S2). <sentence_start/>Non-linear nature of the incident intensity-dependent fluorescence emission confirmed role of two-photon excitation. <sentence_start/>It may be noted that as distance of the fluorescent particle from the fiber increases, the excitation intensity decreases due to divergence of the beam from the fiber and therefore, leads to change in excitation volume.

In order to map the <italic toggle="yes">in-vitro</italic> fiber-optic two-photon activation spectrum of ChR2, the wavelength of the near-infrared stimulation laser beam was tuned from 800 to 900 nm. <sentence_start/>Expression of ChR2 in HEK 293 cells was confirmed by fluorescence imaging of reporter fluorescent protein (YFP). <sentence_start/>The cleaved multimode fiber tip was positioned ∼100 µm away from the clamped-cell. <sentence_start/>In Fig. 1 g, we show representative current responses recorded from a single cell, irradiated with ultrafast NIR laser beam (100 ms pulses, with average power density of 0.02 mW/µm<sup>2</sup>, at cell membrane) at different wavelengths. <sentence_start/>The fiber-optic two-photon activation spectrum of ChR2 (Fig. 1 h) <italic toggle="yes">in-vitro</italic> shows that the peak activation wavelength is at 850 nm. <sentence_start/>Theoretically, two-photon optogenetic excitation is expected to be maximal near 920 nm (double the single photon excitation peak wavelength). <sentence_start/>The current amplitude at 900 nm was 9.9±0.6 pA (n = 18), which was lower than the current amplitude at 850 nm (28.0±2.4 pA, n = 19). <sentence_start/>The observed blue-shift of the two-photon activation spectrum can be attributed to the parity selection rules favoring the two-photon excitation of all-trans-retinal and thus activation of ChR2 (in closed form) to higher energy (open) state than the respective single-photon-induced activation. <sentence_start/>This “blue-shifted” optimum stimulation wavelength for two-photon excitation with respect to single-photon excitation is similar to that observed <citation rid="pone.0111488-Albota1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="18301569" doi="10.1364/ao.37.007352" count="1">[31]</citation>, <citation rid="pone.0111488-Bestvater1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="12423261" doi="10.1046/j.1365-2818.2002.01074.x" count="1">[32]</citation> in two-photon absorption of many fluorescence dyes and in two-photon activation ChR2-sensitized HEK cells <citation rid="pone.0111488-Andrasfalvy1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="20543137" doi="10.1073/pnas.1006620107" pmcid="PMC2900666" count="1">[20]</citation>.
Estimation of two-photon absorption cross section

For estimation of fiber-optic two-photon cross-section of ChR2-activation (Fig. S2), we have considered the dispersion-induced measured pulse-width. <sentence_start/>We estimated the two-photon absorption cross section by fitting the equation to the inward current obtained from patch-clamp as shown in Fig. S2 (a-b). <sentence_start/>The inward increasing current was fitted with following equation,

Where <italic toggle="yes">τ<sub>g</sub></italic> is the ground state life time, defined (2/σ<sub>2</sub> I<sup>2</sup>) for two photon excitation and (1/<italic toggle="yes">σ<sub>1</sub></italic> I) for single photon excitation. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">I</italic> = intensity, <italic toggle="yes">σ<sub>2</sub></italic> = two-photon absorption cross-section, <italic toggle="yes">τ<sub>1</sub></italic> = activation time-constant, and <italic toggle="yes">τ<sub>2</sub></italic> = current decay time-constant.

From the fitted parameters the two photon absorption cross-section at λ = 870 nm and 900 nm was found to be 226.48±5.034 GM and 186.32±33.03 GM respectively. <sentence_start/>This estimated two-photon absorption cross-section is higher than many known fluorophores and is comparable to earlier report <citation rid="pone.0111488-Rickgauer1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19706471" doi="10.1073/pnas.0907084106" pmcid="PMC2736443" count="1">[19]</citation>. <sentence_start/>This is one of the reasons why fiber optics could produce two-photon activation of ChR2 at low average intensities.
Peak of <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> fiber-optic two-photon stimulation wavelength is also blue-shifted

In order to compare the efficacy of two-photon laser beam in stimulating in-depth brain regions <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo,</italic> with that of single-photon, we first theoretically evaluated light propagation in the brain. <sentence_start/>Fig. 3a shows results of Monte Carlo simulations of two-photon (870 nm) light propagation in the two-layered cortex for beam (diameter: 60 µm; laser power: 5 mW) emanating from a fiber having numerical aperture (NA) of 0.15. <sentence_start/>Propagation of a single-photon (470 nm) fiber-optic beam for the same parameters (beam diameter, NA and laser power) is shown in Fig. 3b. <sentence_start/>While it is evident that the near-infrared two-photon beam has a higher penetration depth (even at same power levels), this effect is more profound when (damage-threshold) normalized power levels are compared. <sentence_start/>For <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> two-photon stimulation, besides the input beam characteristics (mode profile, beam size, divergence), the forward scattering nature of the medium (brain) further modulates the beam propagation and thus, impact both axial and transverse stimulation-resolution. <sentence_start/>Fig. S5 shows MC simulation results depicting the effects of different parameters (power, NA, and wavelength) on light propagation in the two-layered cortex. <sentence_start/>For both FO-TPOS (870 nm) and FO-SPOS (470 nm), higher penetration depth was observed with increasing laser beam power (1 to 50 mW) as shown in the XZ-distribution of power density (W/cm<sup>2</sup>) in Fig. S5. <sentence_start/>In our experiments, ∼50 times higher average power density was used in the case of FO-TPOS as compared to that of FO-SPOS. <sentence_start/>Therefore, when results of FO-TPOS with average laser beam power of 50 mW is compared with 1 mW of FO-SPOS, ∼3 times higher penetration depth was observed in case of FO-TPOS for same fiber delivery geometry.

Discussion

The two-photon activation method reported here enabled <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> optogenetic stimulation at depth of 3 mm in the brain. <sentence_start/>Thus, the fiber delivering the FO-TPOS beam could be positioned in superficial cortical layer, leading to minimal invasion into the brain. <sentence_start/>Though from the in-vitro studies, we ruled out the contribution of direct (photothermal or photomechanical) stimulation, we are intrigued by the ability of the NIR ultrafast multimode beam in stimulating deep brain regions. <sentence_start/>We hypothesize that two possibilities can enhance the stimulation efficacy of the NIR fiber-optic beam. <sentence_start/>First, the ChR2 may have non-zero (but small) absorption in NIR spectrum. <sentence_start/>Though single-photon ChR2 activation spectrum has been characterized in visible region, further studies are required to measure single-photon NIR activation of ChR2. <sentence_start/>This would certainly require intense cw light source (average power higher than used in studies reported here) owing to the low activation efficiency in the NIR. <sentence_start/>Secondly, other molecules such as the cofactor (ATR) can absorb NIR light and transfer energy to the opsin by the process of resonance energy transfer (RET).

This non-linear optogenetic approach, combined with electrophysiology and behavioral readout(s) will provide a unique opportunity to dissect the functional neuronal circuitry of deep brain regions. <sentence_start/>Further, this method can be easily integrated with the fiber-optic non-linear endoscopy techniques <citation rid="pone.0111488-Fu1" ref-type="bibr" pmid="19503423" doi="10.1364/oe.14.001027" count="1">[45]</citation> to allow both two-photon stimulation and optical imaging of neural activity <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic>.
Conclusions

Though we characterized two-photon activation efficacy at different near-infrared laser parameters, further studies are required to optimize the fiber-optic two-photon stimulation strategy. <sentence_start/>For example, the large two-photon cross-section of ChR2 should allow use of nanosecond or even microsecond compact near-infrared (NIR) sources for FO-TPOS. <sentence_start/>Further, by selection of right wavelength of the two-photon light source for other opsins such as NpHR (chloride channel), the <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic> FO-TPOS method can be useful for inhibiting neural activity. <sentence_start/>In addition to the demonstrated in-depth stimulation capability of FO-TPOS, high spatial precision in two-photon optogenetic activation should be possible <italic toggle="yes">in-vivo</italic>, by virtue of non-linear nature of ultrafast light-matter interaction. <sentence_start/>Modulation of deep brain regions via FO-TPOS as demonstrated by us, will lead to better understanding of neural circuitry because the technology permits noninvasive and more precise anatomical delivery of stimulation.
